n: A wisdom psalm addressed to everyone in the world. Its message about wealth and death applies to all people, not only Israel.
Rich and poor, important and ordinary — all need to hear this, because death treats everyone the same.

f.g: Literally “sons of Adam and sons of man” — common folk and nobles.

n: The psalmist promises to share wisdom he has thought deeply about.
He will listen for God’s insight and then explain a puzzling riddle to the music of a harp.

f.g: A riddle or puzzle — here, why the wicked rich seem to prosper.
Hebrew mashal — a proverb or comparison.

n: Why should I be afraid when evil people surround me and plot against me?

f.g: Probably “the iniquity of those who dog my heels” — enemies following close behind.

n: These are people who trust in their wealth and brag about how much they have...
...but no amount of money can buy another person out of death. No one can pay God a ransom for a life.
The price of a soul is far too costly — no human could ever pay it. This points to the need for a Redeemer who could pay what we cannot.

f.w: the redemption of their soul is precious
f.g: The ransom for a life is too costly; one must give up on paying it.

n: No one can pay enough to live forever and never see the grave.

f.g: The pit, decay of the grave.

n: Everyone can see that wise people die, as do fools; all leave their wealth to someone else.
The rich imagine their estates will last forever and name their lands after themselves — yet their only lasting home is the grave.

f.w: they call their lands after their own names
f.g: Some ancient versions read “their graves are their homes forever.”

n: A refrain repeated in verse 20: even a person of high honor doesn’t last; he dies like the animals.

f.g: Does not remain, cannot spend the night — he is only passing through.

n: This is the path of the self-confident, yet those who follow them still praise their ideas.
Like sheep herded into a pen, they are led into the grave with death as their shepherd. In the morning — a hint of a future day — the upright will rule over them.

f.g: Death shall shepherd them — a dark reversal of Psalm 23.
Perhaps a hint of resurrection or a coming day of vindication.

n: The great turn of the psalm: no one can ransom himself — but God will ransom me from the grave and take me to himself. This is one of the clearest hopes beyond death in the Old Testament.

f.w: God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave

f.g: He will take me — the same verb used of Enoch being taken.

n: So don’t be intimidated when someone gets rich and his house grows grand.
When he dies, he takes nothing with him; his splendor stays behind.
While alive he congratulated himself, and people praise those who do well for themselves.
Yet he will join his ancestors in the darkness and never see light again.
The refrain returns with a key word added: a person in honor who lacks understanding is like the beasts. Wisdom — knowing God — is what makes the difference.

f.g: Lacks insight — the added word that distinguishes this from verse 12.
